cards.title: A weaker jobs report complicates rate policy
cards.summary: The August 8 issue reports a July payroll decline and downward revisions to prior months. Lower unemployment was partly associated with people leaving the labour force, so it did not on its own establish stronger hiring.

cards.title: Another attempt to remove a Fed governor
cards.summary: The White House renewed its effort to dismiss Lisa Cook over mortgage-related allegations that she disputed. The conflict keeps central-bank independence in focus alongside the inflation debate.

cards.title: Airbnb benefits from stronger guidance
cards.summary: Airbnb shares rose sharply after earnings and an improved full-year outlook, according to the August 8 issue. The result contrasts with the weaker labour-market picture rather than resolving it.

cards.title: Parents remain an important household safety net
cards.summary: The main newsletter’s parenting special describes substantial financial support flowing to adult children and more shared housing. High living costs can shift financial pressure between generations rather than eliminate it.

cards.title: Paid parental leave becomes less generous
cards.summary: The parenting special reports declining employer provision and cutbacks at some large companies. In a softer jobs market, reduced benefits can transfer more of the cost of raising children to households.

cards.title: Walmart raises a warning about spending
cards.summary: Walmart’s US comparable-sales growth slowed to 2.6%, with pharmacy pricing and a softer consumer environment weighing on performance. Its plan to reinvest tariff refunds in lower prices signals continued pressure to defend value-conscious shoppers.

cards.title: Treasury buybacks do not settle the bond market
cards.summary: An expanded debt-buyback programme briefly lowered long-term yields before they rebounded. The newsletter’s account suggests liquidity support alone did not remove investors’ inflation and fiscal concerns.

cards.title: AI changes education decisions before outcomes are clear
cards.summary: Student surveys found many were reconsidering their fields of study because of AI-related job concerns. Changing enrolments and new AI majors show a response to perceived risk, not evidence that any particular degree is future-proof.

cards.title: Evergrande’s collapse brings a criminal sentence
cards.summary: The issue reports a life sentence for founder Hui Ka Yan over financial crimes linked to the property group’s collapse. The case underscores the continuing fallout from the developer’s debt crisis.

cards.title: A packaging dispute pushes Rebel into bankruptcy
cards.summary: Rebel Creamery sought Chapter 11 protection after a $23.8 million judgment in a packaging dispute with Van Leeuwen. The company was appealing, but the liability had already become an immediate financing problem.

cards.title: Canada–US tariffs threaten integrated supply chains
cards.summary: New US duties on Canadian goods prompted a promise of matching retaliation, followed by a threat to raise levies on vehicles, parts and steel. Escalation adds uncertainty for manufacturers ahead of trade-agreement talks.

cards.title: Iran sanctions target the wider trading network
cards.summary: Washington announced immediate sanctions on dozens of targets and threatened broader action against Iran’s trading partners. Implementation, particularly involving China, remained uncertain despite the aggressive rhetoric.

cards.title: Colorado River cuts put farms and construction on notice
cards.summary: A federal proposal would reduce water use in three downstream states while leaving upstream reductions unresolved. Agriculture and property development face planning risk while negotiations and possible litigation continue.

cards.title: Paramount’s takeover faces a remedies test
cards.summary: The newsletter reports preliminary settlement talks over the states’ challenge to Paramount’s planned Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition. A settlement was not assured, and the proposed structural remedies could change the deal’s economics.

cards.title: Bond anxiety revives demand for gold
cards.summary: The August 24 issue describes gold reaching a three-month high as investors worried about government bonds. That links the week’s safe-haven demand to financing and inflation concerns rather than a simple stock-market story.

cards.title: The Fed signals inflation comes first
cards.summary: Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole remarks were interpreted as opening the door to higher interest rates if inflation persists. The issue reports a rise in market-implied hike probabilities, not a policy decision.

cards.title: A possible PayPal deal loses momentum
cards.summary: Stripe and Advent reportedly withdrew from efforts to acquire PayPal for more than $50 billion. The account describes a stalled negotiation, not a completed transaction.

cards.title: Mounjaro gains a cardiovascular indication
cards.summary: The newsletter reports FDA approval to reduce heart attack and stroke risk in adults with Type 2 diabetes. The expanded indication adds another competitive dimension to the GLP-1 market.

cards.title: Payroll estimates face another revision
cards.summary: A preliminary benchmark suggested US employment growth through March was overstated by 79,000 jobs. The adjustment remained provisional and should not be confused with a new monthly jobs loss.

cards.title: A shelved film tests the value of rescued IP
cards.summary: Coyote vs. Acme reached cinemas after Ketchup Entertainment acquired distribution rights to the previously shelved project. Its release illustrates the gap between a studio’s accounting incentives and another distributor’s commercial opportunity.

cards.title: Energy costs spread beyond the petrol pump
cards.summary: The September 8 issue reports record Labor Day petrol and diesel prices as conflict disrupts oil supply. Higher freight and flight costs widen the pressure on households and businesses.

cards.title: Housing faces a fresh financing squeeze
cards.summary: Existing-home sales fell in August while quoted 30-year mortgage rates moved above 7%, according to the September 11 issue. Rising Treasury yields make an already weak housing market harder to finance.

cards.title: A proposed dividend is not an approved payment
cards.summary: Trump proposed $5,000 payments to adults contingent on a Republican election win, but the newsletter describes major funding, inflation and legal objections. Congressional approval would still be needed.

cards.title: Oracle growth keeps AI spending in focus
cards.summary: The September 11 issue reports nearly 30% annual revenue growth at Oracle. The result offers another indicator of demand for computing infrastructure, rather than proof that every AI investment will pay off.

cards.title: AI competition brings new provenance allegations
cards.summary: Anthropic alleged that Moonshot and DeepSeek used intermediary services to route requests to Claude. These are company allegations, not independently established findings; the dispute highlights the commercial stakes of model access.

coverage: Week-to-date through the stated cutoff; only September 29, September 30 and October 2 issues were available. No issues were available for the September 12–25 archive windows.

cards.title: Global bond volatility raises financing pressure
cards.summary: The October 2 issue reports fresh multidecade yield highs before some markets reversed course. Inflation, energy disruption and fiscal deficits were weighing on government debt, with consequences for mortgage and corporate borrowing costs.

cards.title: Oura pauses its stock-market debut
cards.summary: Oura postponed its planned IPO, citing market uncertainty despite reported investor demand. The September 30 issue also reports delays at other issuers, showing that a strong fundraising year does not guarantee an open listing window.

cards.title: AI implementation supports consulting demand
cards.summary: Accenture reported 7% quarterly revenue growth and a stronger outlook, according to the October 2 issue. Demand for help implementing AI is supporting consulting work, although that does not settle the longer-term threat to outsourcing revenue.

cards.title: Nike plans job cuts after another revenue decline
cards.summary: Nike reported a second consecutive quarter of declining revenue as it works to rebuild retail relationships. The company announced plans to reduce headcount, but said specific cuts would not be decided until 2027.

cards.title: Nvidia expands its buyback alongside an AI-security push
cards.summary: The September 29 issue reports an additional $150 billion share-repurchase authorization and the unveiling of OpenShell safeguards for AI agents. Authorization is not completed spending, and Nvidia’s claims about preventing attacks are not independent proof of effectiveness.

coverage: Available-source coverage reconstructed from all seven issues dated October 3–9, including the Delicacy Brew special. The October 9 issue was recovered after the earlier Inbox-only run.

cards.title: Weak hiring sharpens the Fed’s trade-off
cards.summary: The October 3 issue reports just 29,000 additional US jobs in September, unemployment of 4.2% and downward revisions to summer hiring. Minutes covered on October 8 still showed officials anticipating another rate increase this year, with timing dependent on incoming data.

cards.title: Energy relief meets a costly winter forecast
cards.summary: G7 countries and allies agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over four months, according to the October 3 issue. The October 8 issue nevertheless reports an EIA forecast of winter heating-oil prices 34% above the previous year—a forecast, not a realised household bill.

cards.title: New open-weight models target business buyers
cards.summary: Reflection announced Beam while Mistral previewed Large 4 for developers, with a wider release scheduled for October 27. Their claimed capabilities and customisation options could pressure closed-model vendors, but the newsletter did not independently establish performance parity.

cards.title: AI imports widen the US trade deficit
cards.summary: The October 7 issue reports an August trade deficit of $105.6 billion, up 13.7% from July despite tariffs. Imports associated with AI infrastructure, petroleum and gold contributed to the widening gap.

cards.title: Hybrid demand exposes Detroit’s product gap
cards.summary: Asian automakers captured more than half of US new-car purchases in the third quarter, according to the October 5 issue, as demand for hybrids strengthened. Detroit’s limited hybrid range leaves it less able to respond quickly to higher fuel costs.

cards.title: Starbucks–Chipotle takeover talk remains preliminary
cards.summary: The October 9 issue reports that Starbucks explored buying Chipotle, citing the Financial Times, but says no formal offer had been reported. International expansion could be a rationale; a completed deal or agreed terms should not be inferred from the market reaction.

coverage: Available-source coverage reconstructed from all seven issues dated October 10–16, including the Horror Movie Brew special. October 10–11 sources were already archived and were recovered after the earlier Inbox-only run.

cards.title: Inflation increases pressure ahead of the Fed meeting
cards.summary: The October 15 issue reports September consumer inflation of 3.7% and core inflation of 2.6%, both above forecasts, with energy costs feeding through the economy. Market expectations shifted towards a rate increase, but the October 27–28 meeting had not yet taken place.

cards.title: CoreWeave puts AI’s borrowing risk in focus
cards.summary: The October 16 issue describes a sell-off in CoreWeave debt as investors questioned further borrowing on top of a reported $50 billion debt pile. Higher-rate fears and ties to supplier-investor Nvidia intensified scrutiny; market-implied default risk is not a finding that insolvency is inevitable.

cards.title: Russian diesel plan offers uncertain price relief
cards.summary: The October 12 issue reports Trump’s announcement that Russian diesel would reach global markets, while energy experts doubted the proposed volumes would materially lower prices. By October 16, the newsletter reported renewed attacks on Russian refineries after the announced energy ceasefire broke down.

cards.title: Character.AI seeks bankruptcy protection and an asset sale
cards.summary: The October 14 issue reports Character.AI’s bankruptcy amid monetisation problems and legal pressure. A $20 million agreement to sell assets to Disney remained open to higher bids; claims about harmful chatbot behaviour were allegations in lawsuits, not established findings here.

cards.title: Netflix cuts staff as growth slows
cards.summary: Netflix is cutting roughly 1,000 jobs, or 6% of its workforce, according to reporting cited in the October 15 issue. Slower revenue and engagement growth, competition from social video and the enlarged Skydance group raise the pressure on its spending priorities.

cards.title: Low-budget horror becomes a studio talent pipeline
cards.summary: The October 11 editorial special describes studios pursuing YouTube filmmakers and online horror stories after low-budget box-office successes. Lower production costs and existing fan communities can improve the economics, but individual hits do not establish that every project will be profitable.

cards.title: Fuel costs force Delta to cut its outlook
cards.summary: The October 10 issue reports that Delta reduced its full-year earnings forecast despite strong travel demand and growing premium-seat revenue. An unexpectedly large fuel bill illustrates how the energy shock can erode airline margins even when sales rise.

coverage: Available-source coverage of all seven issues dated October 17–23, including the Basketball Brew editorial special. Five material developments retained after ranking; advertisements, quizzes and lower-signal items omitted.

cards.title: AI financing jitters spread to new listings
cards.summary: The October 21 issue reports that South Korean data-centre provider Elice fell 32% on its stock-market debut despite rapid revenue growth. The week’s later issues describe renewed AI-overspending concerns and a tech-stock sell-off, underscoring the gap between infrastructure demand and investors’ willingness to finance it.

cards.title: Critical PHP patches become a deployment priority
cards.summary: The October 22 issue reports a severity-9.2 vulnerability in PHP, a language used by roughly 70% of websites, and urges operators to deploy newly released patches. It describes risks of server-code execution and data theft—not evidence that every PHP site has been compromised.

cards.title: Tesla–SpaceX merger remains exploratory
cards.summary: Musk’s companies formed committees to explore a merger, according to the October 21–22 issues; a combination could be worth roughly $3.5 trillion. No deal was agreed, and the projected valuation and control benefits remain estimates rather than completed outcomes.

cards.title: Meta faces a $25 billion privacy judgment
cards.summary: The October 22 issue reports that a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a consumer-protection case stemming from the Cambridge Analytica data scandal. The judgment follows a jury verdict; it should not be confused with money already paid or a final resolution of all litigation.

cards.title: Fuel and borrowing costs squeeze travel and housing
cards.summary: The October 21 issue reports Thanksgiving airfares up 31% year on year as jet-fuel costs rose, while United cut its profit outlook. It also describes record-low pending home sales and 7.4% mortgage rates, illustrating cost pressure across both discretionary travel and housing.

coverage: Week-to-date through the stated cutoff. Five available issues dated October 25 and October 27–30 were reviewed, including the Morning Boo editorial special; no October 24 or October 26 issue was available in the reviewed source set. Previously published Halloween coverage was consolidated; all five issues count once. Earlier archive coverage gaps are unchanged.

cards.title: Growth strengthens while the Fed holds rates
cards.summary: The October 30 issue reports annualised US GDP growth of 3.4% in Q3, with business investment up 12.7%, while September inflation outpaced income gains and the savings rate fell to 3.8%. The preceding issue reports that the Fed held its benchmark at 3.75%–4.00%, with two dissenters favouring a rise: stronger growth does not remove the inflation constraint.

cards.title: Anthropic files for an IPO, with large spending commitments
cards.summary: The October 27 issue reports that Anthropic filed to list as ANT on Nasdaq, disclosing first-half revenue of $16.3 billion alongside $417 billion of vendor commitments and continued losses. Analysts’ estimate of a possible $100 billion raise is not money already secured; infrastructure demand and governance remain material investor risks.

cards.title: AI adoption has not yet solved Big Tech’s cash-flow equation
cards.summary: The October 29 issue reports that Google’s AI Mode monetised less effectively than traditional search and Alphabet recorded negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion despite cloud strength. The October 30 issue adds that Amazon missed revenue and earnings expectations and also reported negative free cash flow, while Alphabet shares fell 12.64%.

cards.title: DoorDash announces a $17 billion Instacart acquisition
cards.summary: After the October 28 issue described talks, the October 30 newsletter reports an announced $17 billion agreement joining major restaurant- and grocery-delivery platforms. DoorDash was expected to retain Instacart’s brand and technology after closing; an announced acquisition is not a completed merger.

cards.title: Halloween creates earlier retail demand and paid convenience
cards.summary: The October 25 special cites an NRF forecast of $13.5 billion in US Halloween spending and says about a quarter of shoppers bought seasonal goods by early August, letting retailers bridge quiet periods and reduce warehouse storage. It also describes porch-decorating services charging a few hundred dollars to $2,000, with some expanding or franchising—examples of demand, not guaranteed growth for every operator.
